The extended pre-reproductive phase may confer advantages by allowing females to accumulate sufficient fat reserves, which are critical for surviving hibernation and supporting the energetic demands of gestation and lactation upon emergence. Maximum lifespan estimates for the Woodland jumping mouse approach 4 years [am = 4 years] under captive conditions maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], although data from wild populations remain uncertain and likely reflect higher mortality rates due to predation and environmental stress. The species occupies moist coniferous and mixed forests across northeastern North America, where it feeds primarily on mycorrhizal fungi, supplemented by seeds and arthropods. Its dependence on hypogeous fungi links it intimately to forest ecosystem health, as the mouse serves as a key vector for spore dispersal. Conservation efforts must therefore consider the broader habitat requirements that sustain both the mouse and its fungal food sources across the landscape.
